title: A Quantitative Fluorescence Microscopy-based Single Liposome Assay for Detecting the Compositional Inhomogeneity Between Individual Liposomes
protocol: Weigh out POPC, cholesterol, DOPE-Atto488, DOPE-Atto655, and DSPE-PEG2000-biotin.
Dissolve POPC in tert-butanol:water (9:1) to 50 mM.
Dissolve cholesterol in tert-butanol:water (9:1) to 25 mM.
Dissolve DOPE-Atto488 in tert-butanol:water (9:1) to 0.1 mM.
Dissolve DOPE-Atto655 in tert-butanol:water (9:1) to 0.1 mM.
Dissolve DSPE-PEG2000-biotin in tert-butanol:water (9:1) to 0.1 mM.
Heat lipids to 55 °C for complete dissolution.
Mix POPC, cholesterol, DOPE-Atto488, DOPE-Atto655, and DSPE-PEG2000-biotin at a molar ratio of 68.95:30:0.5:0.5:0.05.
Add 138 µL of POPC to the mixture.
Add 120 µL of cholesterol to the mixture.
Add 500 µL of DOPE-Atto488 to the mixture.
Add 500 µL of DOPE-Atto655 to the mixture.
Add 50 µL of DSPE-PEG-biotin to the mixture.
Loosen the lid of the glass vial containing lipids.
Snap-freeze the vial in liquid nitrogen.
Lyophilize the frozen lipid mixture overnight.
Add 1 mL of 200 mM D-sorbitol buffer (sorbitol buffer) to the dry lipids.
Heat the mixture to 45 °C and expose to magnetic stirring for at least 1 h.
Freeze the lipid suspension by dipping the vial in liquid nitrogen.
Wait until the suspension is completely frozen.
Dip the frozen suspension in a heating bath at 55 °C until the mixture is completely thawed.
Repeat steps of freezing and thawing until the liposome suspension has been exposed to a total of 11 freeze/thaw cycles.
Prepare bovine serum albumin (BSA; 1 mg/mL) in HEPES buffer.
Prepare BSA-biotin (1 mg/mL) in HEPES buffer.
Prepare streptavidin (0.025 mg/mL) in HEPES buffer.
Mix 1,200 µL of BSA with 120 µL of BSA-biotin.
Add 300 μL of the mixture to each well in an 8-well slide for microscopy.
Incubate the slide for 20 min at room temperature (RT).
Wash the slide 8 times with 300 μL of HEPES buffer.
Add 250 μL of streptavidin and incubate for 10 min at RT.
Repeat the 8 washes described in step 2.4.
Store the microscope slide with 300 μL of sorbitol buffer in each well at 4 °C.
Dilute the liposome suspension to about 20 µM total lipid in sorbitol buffer.
Place the slide on the microscope and focus on the surface of the chamber using the increased laser reflection signal from the glass/buffer interface as a guide.
Wash the chamber 4 times with 300 μL of fresh HEPES buffer.
Take out 100 µL of buffer from the chamber.
Add the extracted buffer to a microcentrifuge tube containing 10 µL of diluted liposome stock (20 µM total lipid).
Mix properly and return 110 µL back into the chamber.
Put the specimen under the microscope.
Use a rudimental microscope setting capable of detecting signal from the liposome fluorophore(s) to observe the liposomes being immobilized on the surface.
Aim for a liposome surface density that is simultaneously sparse enough to identify individual liposomes and dense enough that it facilitates high-throughput measurements.
Typically using a 50 µm x 50 µm field of view, aim for 300−400 liposomes per frame.
Wash the chamber 3x with 200 µL of HEPES buffer once an appropriate liposome surface density is reached.
Set up the microscope for imaging single liposomes.
Use a high greyscale resolution for imaging.
Apply a pixel scheme allowing oversampling of individual liposomes.
Select a bit depth of 16 and at least 1,024 x 1,024 pixels for a 50 µm x 50 µm area.
Apply line-averaging if available to reduce noise (e.g., 3 scans per line).
Choose an excitation laser power that ensures nonsignificant frame-to-frame bleaching and strong signal.
Ensure the signal is clear enough to discriminate individual liposomes from the background.
Make sure detectors are not saturated to avoid bias in intensity quantification.
Image the DOPE-Atto488 fluorophore by exciting at 488 nm and reading emission at 495−560 nm.
Image the DOPE-Atto655 fluorophore by exciting at 633 nm and reading emission at 660−710 nm.
Ensure each channel is imaged sequentially to avoid cross-excitation.
Acquire at least 10 images of the sample, covering different areas of the surface.
Image at least 3,000 individual liposomes per sample area.
Refocus the microscope for every new image acquisition.
Name image files so that pairs with the same liposomes in different fluorescence channels can be easily identified during data analysis.
Image the same area of liposomes before and after refocusing to quantify experimental uncertainty.
Export images from the microscope software as .tiff files.
Export the two channels of the same liposomes individually.
Load the corresponding pair of .tiff images of two different fluorescence channels in the same imaging field into FIJI software.
Choose Color, and use the Merge Channel function to create a composite of the two channels.
Observe if the liposomes imaged in two different channels display good colocalization or whether visible drift occurred.
In case of drift between the two fluorescence channels, translate one of the frames using the Transform > Translate function.
Ensure the ComDet plugin (v.0.3.6.1 or newer) is installed.
Open the ComDet plugin to detect particles by going to Plugins menu and choosing ComDet v.0.3.6.1 > Detect Particles.
In ComDet, choose the Detect Particles on Both Channels Individually function.
Set the Max Distance Between Co-localized Spots similar to the Approximate Particle Size.
Set the Sensitivity of Detection in both channels to Very Dim Particles (SNR = 3).
Check the boxes for Calculate Colocalization and Plot Detected Particles in Both Channels.
Press OK to start the analysis.
Export the data table Results containing colocalization data to a data handling software by saving it as a .txt file.
Import the exported .txt file into the chosen data handling software.
Filter the data so only Abs_frame = 1 is plotted.
Take out part of the liposome stock.
Extrude the liposomes 21 times through a 50 nm polycarbonate filter.
Dilute the extruded liposomes by adding 10 μL of liposome suspension to 800 μL of sorbitol buffer in a microcentrifuge tube.
Transfer diluted liposome sample to a polypropylene single-use cuvette.
Measure the size using dynamic light scattering (DLS).
Perform at least three independent runs to measure the size and polydispersity of the liposome suspension.
Image the calibration liposomes on the microscope using exactly the same experimental settings as defined in steps 4.1 and 4.2.
Extract the integrated intensity for each calibration liposome in the calibration images.
Extract the filtered results sheet containing liposome fluorescence intensities as described in steps 5.1−5.10.
From the results table, extract the "IntegratedInt" column.

Because the total integrated intensity of a liposome labeled in its membrane is proportional to the surface area of the liposome and is thus proportional to the square of its diameter, plot a square root intensity histogram of the fluorescence intensity of the calibration liposomes.
Fit the integrated intensity histogram produced with a log normal distribution and extract the average fluorescence intensity of the calibration liposomes.

To determine the relation between the square root intensity (IntSqrt) and liposome size, calculate the correction factor (C) using the average liposome diameter (Dia) weighed by the number obtained from the DLS measurements: Dia = C x IntSqrt is equivalent to C = Dia / IntSqrt.
Calculate IntSqrt values for the liposomes in the compositional inhomogeneity experiment.
Convert these IntSqrt values to diameters by multiplying with the correction factor.
Plot the intensity ratio value as a function of diameter for the compositional inhomogeneity liposomes.
